title: Should You Sell Your Stocks Right Now? Here's What a Century's Worth of History Suggests.
detail:
Should You Sell Your Stocks Right Now? Here's What a Century's Worth of History Suggests.
Jennifer Saibil, The Motley Fool
Sun, November 1, 2026 at 12:35 PM CST 5 min read
^GSPC
NVDA
Trade NVIDIA on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

The forerunner of today's S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) goes back to 1926, when the S&P 90 was created as a stock market index. It was changed to 500 companies in 1957, and as of this year, there's a century's worth of data to inform investors about historical trends.

That small start 100 years ago preceded the worst stock market crash in U.S. history, but a century later, the index is thriving, even though it's had its ups and downs over the decades.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Is there eventually going to be another down? Most certainly. Should you sell your stocks beforehand? Like most things in life, it depends. Here's what you need to know.

The S&P 500 is at record levels

The S&P 500 is up 13% this year and hit its most recent record on Oct. 6. If it remains this way by the end of the year, it will be the fourth year in a row with double-digit gains.

Image source: Getty Images.

Many of those gains are due to the massive tech companies that anchor the index. It's weighted, which means that the largest stocks by market cap account for the most weight. Nvidia, Apple, Microsoft, Amazon, and Alphabet are its top five stocks by weight, and there isn't a non-artificial intelligence (AI) stock in the top 10. 39.7% of the index is concentrated in tech stocks, which means it's highly exposed to changes in AI and the tech sector.

Today's enthusiasm for AI stocks is to some degree propping up the rest of the market, but the economy as a whole has been robust despite inflation. Companies have been reporting strong growth, leading to confidence in their stocks. However, prices are outpacing growth, leading to an expensive market.

Should you sell before the fall?

There are signs that a crash could potentially happen soon. The CAPE ratio, which measures the average 10-year adjusted price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio, is at its second-highest level ever at almost 41. When it reached a record of 44 in 2000, the market crashed. It didn't reach its previous high until seven years later.

The AI build-out is eerily reminiscent of the dot-com bubble at that time. While the S&P 500 is reaching highs, and with the prospect of a fall, you might be tempted to sell your stocks and pocket your gains. But that's a flawed argument.

First, no one knows when the crash is coming. There could be another year, or more, before it happens. If you sell now, you'll lose the chance to see your stocks continue to compound. Even if the market crashes, selling now means you miss the chance to see your stocks rebound and go even higher. As the saying goes, time in, not timing, the market is what matters.

The Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (NYSEMKT: VOO) has always been one of the best long-term investments for everyday, regular folks. But there are some legitimate questions about whether now is the right time to invest. Is it too top-heavy? Is it too concentrated in tech? Is it primed for a pullback given how far it's risen in the past few years?

Currently, it has roughly 40% of the index invested in tech stocks. Almost 40% is accounted for just by the top 10 holdings. Both are historically high figures, which makes the S&P 500 less diversified than at almost any other point in its history.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

Despite this, I believe the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF remains one of the best long-term investment options. A big part of the reason why is the same reason it's become historically concentrated -- its market-cap weighting methodology.

That strategy helps the index evolve over time in line with the state of the U.S. economy. At different points in history, railroads, energy, financials, and now technology have been the biggest sector allocations. If something else emerges in the future, the index composition will likely change again to give that greater weighting. The S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) essentially reconstitutes itself over time.

Plus, let's not forget that it includes hundreds of the biggest and most successful companies in the United States. That makes an ideal portfolio cornerstone in almost any situation. There will be times when it's concentrated, where it'll underperform, or it'll experience a 20% to 30% drawdown. That's just part of what the S&P 500 is and does.

But it's still a great long-term investment.

How Many AGNC Shares It Takes to Earn $500 a Month in Dividends
Matt DiLallo, The Motley Fool

AGNC
NVDA
^GSPC

AGNC Investment (NASDAQ: AGNC) currently yields 16.3%. That's more than 10 times higher than the S&P 500, which currently yields 1.1%. That supercharged yield enables you to generate much more dividend income at a lower investment rate.

Here's a look at how many shares of the mortgage REIT you'd need to own to produce $500 of dividend income each month.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.
It's all about risk and reward

AGNC Investment currently pays a monthly dividend of $0.12 per share. At that rate, you'd need to hold almost 4,167 shares to generate $500 a month in dividend income, which would cost about $36,667 at its recent share price.

For perspective, you'd need to invest roughly $571,429 into an S&P 500 index fund to produce the same amount of income. That's a staggering 94% less capital for the same income.

However, there's a catch. AGNC's much higher-yielding dividend comes with an equally elevated risk profile. The REIT invests solely in Agency MBS (pools of residential mortgages guaranteed against credit losses by government agencies like Fannie Mae) on a leveraged basis. That leverage boosts returns and its risk profile.

As long as its returns remain above its costs, the REIT can maintain its dividend. That's currently the case. CEO Peter Federico noted on AGNC's third-quarter conference call that its investment returns in current market conditions are above its costs, making its dividend "well-aligned with the economics of our business."

The issue is that it has experienced misalignment before. When that happens, the REIT has had to reduce its dividend. It last cut its payout in 2020 from $0.16 per share to its current rate.

There's no doubt that you can currently generate a lot of dividend income each month from an investment in AGNC. However, you need to realize that it's not a bankable income stream. As a result, you shouldn't invest the nearly $37,000 it would take to produce $500 a month of dividend income from the REIT unless that were a very small percentage of your overall portfolio.

The artificial intelligence (AI) boom is creating opportunities beyond tech giants. Astera Labs (NASDAQ: ALAB), Credo Technology Group (NASDAQ: CRDO), and Sanmina (NASDAQ: SANM) are three promising companies benefiting from rising AI spending. None of the three was added to the S&P 500 in September, and the next rebalance should take effect Dec. 21.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

To be included in the S&P 500, a company requires a market capitalization of at least $22.7 billion and positive earnings. If AI spending continues to drive massive growth, these stocks could emerge as future S&P 500 candidates, potentially rewarding investors who get in early.

Astera Labs, the largest of the three by market value, comes first.

Image source: Getty Images.
1. Connectivity chips are driving Astera Labs' rapid growth

Astera Labs develops connectivity solutions that move data between chips, memory, and other components in AI systems. As these systems become more complex, the connections between them can become a bottleneck. Astera's products are addressing that challenge. The company is already expanding beyond its established connectivity products.

Its Scorpio fabric switches help connect large numbers of AI chips, while its optical connectivity and custom solutions offer greater opportunities as AI data centers evolve.

With Astera, investors demand solid growth, as evidenced by the stock's forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of almost 45 times. But the results are already showing up in earnings.

Astera has also attracted attention as a potential S&P 500 addition; in fact, its $45 billion market cap already clears S&P's $22.7 billion minimum. The main risk, however, is that its growth depends heavily on AI spending, while competition and changing connectivity standards could challenge its position.

Meanwhile, another company is tackling the broader challenge of moving data across advanced AI data centers.

2. Optical products could widen Credo's reach in AI data centers

Credo develops high-speed connectivity products spanning copper and optical solutions, helping customers move data reliably across AI infrastructure. Its portfolio includes active electrical cables, optical digital signal processors, and other networking products.

One of the most interesting developments is Credo's expansion into optical connectivity. Although copper is useful for short-distance connections, optical technology can become more attractive as data rates and transmission distances grow. This gives the company broad exposure to various networking hardware used in AI data centers.

title: Prediction: A Bear Market Is Coming, and This 1 Investing Move Will Make or Break Your Portfolio

Prediction: A Bear Market Is Coming, and This 1 Investing Move Will Make or Break Your Portfolio

If I scream "a bear market is coming!" it will certainly seem alarming. But the proper response to that is really to nod knowingly and to move on -- because a bear market is coming, at some point.

Stock market corrections, crashes, and bear markets simply recur. Fortunately, though, the market and our economy have always recovered after each one, eventually hitting new highs.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

So given that a bear market is likely coming -- perhaps this year or next -- what should you do? Well, be sure that your money is parked in the right places.

Image source: Getty Images.

First, check out how the S&P 500 has performed in recent years:

Considering that the stock market's long-term average annual gains have been close to 10%, those are a lot of outsize gains. Also, note that bear markets happen, on average, every 3.5 years, per Hartford Funds, with the average one lasting less than a year. So it's more than reasonable to expect a bear market this year or next, and to expect it to not last too long -- though it might.

Is your money parked in the right places?

The big question, then, is how you as an investor should deal with this situation.

My main piece of advice would be to have your money parked in the right places. And by that, I mean your short-term money -- funds that you expect to need within five years or so -- should not be in the stock market, as it's a volatile place. If there's a market crash and a bear market that lasts, say, three or more years, you don't want the accounts you planned to draw from to have temporarily shrunk. Short-term money can be stored in high-yield savings accounts, certificates of deposit (CDs), money market accounts, and bonds.

To be more conservative, you might keep money you'll need within 10 years in a less volatile place. And if you're approaching retirement, you might move a larger chunk of your portfolio out of stocks -- though remember that if you're, say, 60 and you might live for 25 more years, much of your nest egg will be remaining invested for many years, so keeping some of your portfolio in stocks should serve you well.

title: History Says Now Is the Perfect Time to Buy Nvidia Stock

History Says Now Is the Perfect Time to Buy Nvidia Stock
Keithen Drury, The Motley Fool

NVDA
^GSPC

Trading disclosure

2026 hasn't been the best year for Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA). While it's up 13% versus 11% from the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC), Nvidia investors don't expect market-beating performance; they expect market-crushing performance. When you look at Nvidia's results, it's easy to see it should be doing better, as it grew revenue at 106% in the second quarter (Q2).

Over the long term, company growth and stock performance tend to be highly correlated, so what's up with the disconnect? I believe it's just the market lagging behind, and history tells us that right now is an incredible buying opportunity.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Nvidia is trading at a major discount

The best way to value Nvidia from a current and historical perspective is to utilize the forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio. This metric uses analysts' estimates for the full fiscal year to price the stock, so it bakes in some growth. At the start of a fiscal year, these measures tend to look pretty cheap, as there is a full year's worth of growth ahead. When you get halfway through the fiscal year (Q3 results aren't available yet), this starts to become a more conservative estimate, as only six months of growth are projected. So, sometimes stocks start to look a tad expensive toward the end of the year.

In both 2024 and 2025, Nvidia's stock reached 40 times forward earnings before the year was over. That's not the case this year.

NVDA PE Ratio (Forward) data by YCharts.

At just under 23 times forward earnings, Nvidia hasn't seen the end-of-year rally it normally does. This raises the question of why, and I think it's simply because the market is trying to call Nvidia's bluff (even if it's wrong). The S&P 500 trades at about 19.2 times forward earnings, so Nvidia trades at only a slight premium to the broader market. This is essentially the market conveying that after this year, it expects market-average growth from Nvidia.

But according to Nvidia and Wall Street analysts, that's a gross error. Nvidia itself told investors during its Q2 earnings call that it expects 70% revenue growth next year. It's rare for a company to provide next-year guidance six months before the year begins, but it shows the confidence Nvidia has in its future growth. This is likely because many of its clients have locked in orders for next year, giving it high visibility of what's to come. Wall Street analysts are also bullish, expecting 68% revenue growth next fiscal year.

(Bloomberg) -- The stock market got a long-awaited jolt of volatility late last week after disappointing earnings from technology giants added to angst around the AI-driven rally.

Most Read from Bloomberg

Ray-Ban Heir Rejects $3.9 Billion Offer for Stake in Family Firm

WSJ Wins Dismissal of Trump's $10 Billion Defamation Suit

Binance Estimates $6.3 Billion Hacked in Crypto's Biggest Heist

Apple Overtakes Nvidia to Become World's Most Valuable Company

Valero to Buy, Restart Idled Texas Refinery as Fuel Rallies

Now traders are bracing for further shocks this week from the US midterm elections and Nvidia Corp. earnings later in November.

The Cboe Volatility Index on Friday touched the highest intraday level since April as the S&P 500 dropped the most since June. The premium for puts protecting against further losses also surged, as did correlations among stocks, which can signal broader stress in the market. Still, those measures remain well below the levels in March after the US and Israel attacked Iran.

With Nvidia due to report earnings, following disappointing results from Amazon.com Inc., Alphabet Inc. and Intel Corp., investors are preparing for more episodes of volatility. Traders are also eyeing US midterm election results for the potential effect on the war in Iran and domestic economic policy.

"This looks more like a bullish rotation with a derating at its core than the beginning of a broad market deterioration.," said Florian Ielpo, head of macro research at Lombard Odier Investment Management.

So far, the latest selloff has been largely focused on the technology sector, with investors rotating away from the high-flying firms that led the gains this year. Realized 60-day volatility on the US benchmark last week touched the lowest in more than a year, with the low correlation this year and tendency of zero-day options traders to buy dips and sell rallies helping to restrain moves.

The late-week slide comes in a year that's been relatively placid. While 2025 saw a cluster of extreme market swings around the tariff tumult in April, in 2026 US stocks have largely shrugged off spikes in oil prices and interest rates.

But even as the technology-heavy Nasdaq 100 capped its worst month since 2025, some investors were betting on a recovery. There were pockets of call and call spread buying seen Friday on the benchmark indexes and some of the most beaten-down tech names such as Intel.

Options were relatively pricey before the larger gyrations late in the week, with the VIX at the higher end of the range over the past five years compared with 20-day realized swings.
